question: we're on AWS EC2 -- is there a specific mitigation against SSRF being abused to steal instance credentials from the metadata service?
answer: Yes -- migrate to IMDSv2 and disable the old IMDSv1. IMDSv2 is a defense-in-depth mechanism for AWS that mitigates some instances of SSRF being used to access and steal credentials and access tokens from the instance metadata service.
source_section: IMDSv2 in AWS
source_passage:
In cloud environments SSRF is often used to access and steal credentials and access tokens from metadata services (e.g. AWS Instance Metadata Service, Azure Instance Metadata Service, GCP metadata server).

[IMDSv2](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/defense-in-depth-open-firewalls-reverse-proxies-ssrf-vulnerabilities-ec2-instance-metadata-service/) is an additional defense-in-depth mechanism for AWS that mitigates some of the instances of SSRF.

To leverage this protection migrate to IMDSv2 and disable old IMDSv1.

question: our webhook feature lets customers register a callback URL that our server later POSTs to -- since we can't allowlist arbitrary customer URLs ahead of time, what step-by-step validation should happen before that outbound request actually fires?
answer: Reject the request unless every one of these checks passes: (1) validate that the supplied value is a well-formed IP address or domain name; (2) apply a block-list check -- for an IP, verify it's a public address; for a domain, verify it resolves as public (not via an internal-only resolver) and then re-validate every A/AAAA address it resolves to as public, binding the connection to that validated address; (3) validate the requested protocol against an allowlist of HTTP/HTTPS only; (4) validate the token parameter name against a strict character set; (5) validate the token value against a strict character set; (6) validate any other business data needed for the call; then (7) build the HTTP POST request using only that validated information, connect only to the IP address already validated in step 2, and disable redirect-following in the HTTP client.
source_section: Cases > Case 2 - Application can send requests to ANY external IP address or domain name > Available protections > Application layer
source_passage:
**Validation flow (if one the validation steps fail then the request is rejected):**

1. The application will receive the IP address or domain name of the *TargetedApplication* and it will apply the first validation on the input data using the libraries/regex mentioned in this [section](Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md#application-layer).
2. The second validation will be applied against the IP address or domain name of the *TargetedApplication* using the following block-list approach:
   - For IP address:
     - The application will verify that it is a public one (see the hint provided in the next paragraph with the python code sample).
   - For domain name:
        1. The application will verify that it is a public one by trying to resolve the domain name against the DNS resolver that will only resolve internal domain name. Here, it must return a response indicating that it do not know the provided domain because the expected value received must be a public domain.
        2. Retrieve all the IP addresses behind the domain name (records *A* + *AAAA* for IPv4 + IPv6) and apply the same public-address verification described above. Bind the connection to a validated address as described under [domain name validation](#domain-name); checking DNS answers separately does not prevent DNS rebinding.
3. The application will receive the protocol to use for the request via a dedicated input parameter for which it will verify the value against an allowed list of protocols (`HTTP` or `HTTPS`).
4. The application will receive the parameter name for the token to pass to the *TargetedApplication* via a dedicated input parameter for which it will only allow the characters set `[a-z]{1,10}`.
5. The application will receive the token itself via a dedicated input parameter for which it will only allow the characters set `[a-zA-Z0-9]{20}`.
6. The application will receive and validate (from a security point of view) any business data needed to perform a valid call.
7. The application will build the HTTP POST request **using only validated information** and connect only to an IP address validated in step 2 (*don't forget to disable the support for [redirection](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Redirections) in the web client used*).

question: What's the actual fix for mass assignment — is it enough to just blocklist a sensitive field like 'isAdmin', or what's the recommended approach?
answer: Blocklisting a specific field like isAdmin is not the recommended approach, because a new or overlooked sensitive field stays bindable. Instead, prefer dedicated input objects (DTOs) that only contain the fields a caller may edit, and explicitly allow-list which fields can be bound when binding to an object that has additional properties.
source_section: Introduction > Solutions
source_passage:
- Prefer dedicated input objects, such as Data Transfer Objects (DTOs), containing only fields the caller may edit; see [Spring's model design guidance](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/web/webmvc/mvc-data-binding.html).
- Explicitly allow-list fields when binding to an object with additional properties.
- Do not rely on a block-list as the sole protection: a new or overlooked sensitive field remains bindable. [CWE-915 recommends allowlists over denylists](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/915.html). The block-list examples below illustrate mechanisms encountered in existing applications, not the recommended design.

question: Our pen test report flagged both an IDOR and a mass assignment finding on the same /update_profile endpoint and called them 'the same root cause.' Is that actually accurate?
answer: Not quite — they're related access-control gaps but not identical. IDOR means the app is missing an object-level authorization check: a user supplies a reference (ID, UUID, token, etc.) to an object and the app never verifies they're allowed to access or manipulate that specific object. Mass assignment is a different mechanism: a framework auto-binds incoming request parameters straight into an object's fields, so an attacker can set fields they were never meant to control (like isAdmin) even on an object they ARE authorized to update.
source_section: Introduction
source_passage:
There are three ingredients to an IDOR:

1. An **object** such as an account, document, support ticket, transaction or partner profile.
2. A **reference** to that object in the form of an ID, UUID, account number, token or slug.
3. A **missing object-level authorization check** that allows a user to access or manipulate an object they should not be able to access.

extra_sources.source_passage:
Software frameworks sometimes allow developers to automatically bind HTTP request parameters into program code variables or objects to make using that framework easier on developers. This can sometimes cause harm.

Attackers can sometimes use this methodology to create new parameters that the developer never intended which in turn creates or overwrites new variable or objects in program code that was not intended.

This is called a **Mass Assignment** vulnerability.

question: Before we ship this feature, how should we actually test that object-level access control is enforced everywhere, instead of just eyeballing the code?
answer: Create two test user accounts (User A and User B), create objects owned by each one (documents, support tickets, invoices, etc.), then authenticate as User A and try to access User B's objects by modifying the object references in requests. Verify access is denied regardless of whether the identifier is predictable or hard to guess.
source_section: Verifying access controls
source_passage:
1. Create User A and User B.
2. Create objects owned by each user (documents, support tickets, invoices, etc.).
3. Authenticate as User A and attempt to access User B's objects by modifying object references in requests.
4. Verify that the application denies unauthorized access regardless of whether the object identifier is predictable or unguessable.

question: Leadership wants to skip MFA and just rely on CAPTCHA plus IP blocking for login abuse. What's the actual data point this cheat sheet cites for how effective MFA is against this kind of attack?
answer: Analysis by Microsoft suggests MFA would have stopped 99.9% of account compromises, which is why the cheat sheet calls it by far the best defense against credential stuffing and password spraying.
source_section: Multi-Factor Authentication
source_passage: [Multi-factor authentication (MFA)](Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.md) is by far the best defense against the majority of password-related attacks, including credential stuffing and password spraying, with analysis by Microsoft suggesting that it would have stopped [99.9% of account compromises](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/Azure-Active-Directory-Identity/Your-Pa-word-doesn-t-matter/ba-p/731984).

question: I've got two separate worries: someone cracking stored password hashes, and someone hijacking a session via a predictable or fixated session ID. Is that the same OWASP guidance, or do I need to look in two different places?
answer: They are covered by different sheets. The Password Storage Cheat Sheet addresses offline password guessing by recommending slow password hashes such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with unique salts, rather than plaintext or fast SHA-256. The Session Management Cheat Sheet identifies disclosure, capture, prediction, brute force, and fixation of a session ID as paths to session hijacking. One concerns stored credentials; the other concerns an active authenticated session.
source_section: Password Storage Cheat Sheet > Introduction
source_passage: Passwords should never be stored in plain text. Instead, they must be protected using strong, slow hashing algorithms such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or PBKDF2. A unique salt must be added to each password to prevent attackers from using precomputed lookup tables like rainbow tables. Fast hashing algorithms such as SHA‑256 are not suitable for password storage because they allow attackers to perform large numbers of guesses quickly.

extra_sources.source_passage: The disclosure, capture, prediction, brute force, or fixation of the session ID will lead to session hijacking (or sidejacking) attacks, where an attacker is able to fully impersonate a victim user in the web application.

review_notes: Removed session-ID generation and regeneration advice that was not in the cited Session Management introduction.

question: What's the lowest-memory Argon2id setting OWASP still considers acceptable if I'm tight on RAM?
answer: The lowest-memory configuration listed is m=7168 (7 MiB), t=5, p=1. All five listed configurations (46/19/12/9/7 MiB paired with t=1 through t=5 respectively) provide an equivalent level of defense -- the only trade-off is between CPU time and RAM usage.
source_section: Password Storage Cheat Sheet > Password Hashing Algorithms > Argon2id
source_passage:
Tune memory and iteration costs to make password cracking expensive while keeping authentication practical under expected load. [Benchmark the chosen parameters on the target system](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106.html#section-4); increasing parallelism is not a guarantee of slower password guessing. Use one of the following minimum configurations:

- m=47104 (46 MiB), t=1, p=1 (Do not use with Argon2i)
- m=19456 (19 MiB), t=2, p=1 (Do not use with Argon2i)
- m=12288 (12 MiB), t=3, p=1
- m=9216 (9 MiB), t=4, p=1
- m=7168 (7 MiB), t=5, p=1

These configuration settings provide an equal level of defense, and the only difference is a trade off between CPU and RAM usage.
review_notes: This source is an explanatory bullet list, not code or a table, so corrected the row type to factual; included the introduction and trade-off sentence supporting acceptable minimum and equivalence.

question: When I build password-reset tokens, do the security rules basically mirror what I'd do for stored passwords, or is there something different about handling a reset token?
answer: They share the need for secure storage, but the cited guidance does not prescribe the same hashing method for both. Passwords should be stored using strong, slow hashes with a unique salt. Password-reset tokens should be generated with a cryptographically safe random generator, be long enough to resist brute force, be stored securely, and additionally be single-use and expire after an appropriate period.
source_section: Forgot Password Cheat Sheet > Introduction
source_passage:
- **Ensure that generated tokens or codes are:**
    - **Randomly generated using a cryptographically safe algorithm.**
    - **Sufficiently long to protect against brute-force attacks.**
    - **Stored securely.**
    - **Single use and expire after an appropriate period.**

extra_sources.source_passage: Passwords should never be stored in plain text. Instead, they must be protected using strong, slow hashing algorithms such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or PBKDF2. A unique salt must be added to each password to prevent attackers from using precomputed lookup tables like rainbow tables.

review_notes: Removed the inference that slow hashing matters less for reset tokens; the cited password source discusses password storage, while the reset-token source specifies secure storage without comparing algorithms.

question: I'm storing the secrets my GitHub Actions pipeline needs. Combining the general secrets-management guidance with the GitHub-Actions-specific guidance, what should I actually be doing with them?
answer: From Secrets Management: rotate CI/CD-stored secrets regularly, and explicitly validate that forking the repository or copying a job definition does not copy the secret along with it. From GitHub Actions Security: when calling a reusable workflow, don't use `secrets: inherit` (it passes every secret the caller has, including ones the called workflow doesn't need) — explicitly pass only the specific secrets that workflow requires.
source_section: Secrets Management Cheat Sheet > 3 Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) > 3.2 Where should a secret be? > 3.2.1 As part of your CI/CD tooling
source_passage:
- Rotation: Regularly rotate secrets.
- Forking should not leak: Validate that a fork of the repository or copy of the job definition does not copy the secret.

extra_sources.source_section: GitHub Actions Security Cheat Sheet > Write Secure GitHub Workflows > Protect secrets used in workflows > Eliminate `secrets: inherit` while reusing workflows
extra_sources.source_passage: When invoking a reusable workflow, `secrets: inherit` passes all secrets available to the calling workflow, including secrets the called workflow may not need. [Explicitly pass only the required secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/reuse-workflows#using-inputs-and-secrets-in-a-reusable-workflow).

question: This cheat sheet buckets supply-chain threats into four broad categories. What are they?
answer: Source code threats, build environment threats, dependency-related threats, and deployment and runtime threats.
source_section: Software Supply Chain Security > Overview of Threat Landscape
source_passage:
- Source code threats. These type of threats focus on violating the integrity of a source code which is then built and and deployed or potentially consumed by other software projects. Threats in this category include VCS exploits, the introduction of malicious or vulnerable code into a codebase, or building code from an unauthorized branch.
- Build environment threats. These threats modify a software artifact but without altering the underlying source code or exploiting the build process itself. Examples include build cache poisoning, compromising a privileged account used by the build tool, or publishing software built from an untrusted source.
- Dependency related threats. Threats that result from the consumption of both direct and transitive software dependencies. The most common threat is using a vulnerable or compromised dependency.
- Deployment and runtime threats. These threats exploit either the deployment process or runtime environment. Common examples include compromising a privilege CI/CD account, software misconfigurations, and deployment of compromised binaries.

question: Before I pull in some open-source library for a project, what questions should I actually be asking to vet it from a security angle?
answer: Among others: Is the project actively maintained? Is it sufficiently popular/well-known in its community? Is it mature? Is the version you'd use an actual release (not alpha/beta)? Does it have enough maintainers/contributors for its complexity? Does it keep its own dependencies updated? Does it have solid test coverage including security-relevant tests? Is it well-documented, including secure-usage guidance? Does it have an established, documented vulnerability-reporting process with timely fixes? And is your intended use consistent with its license?
source_section: Software Supply Chain Security > Mitigations and Security Best Practices > Mitigating Dependency Threats > Assess Suppliers
source_passage:
- Is the project actively maintained?
- Is the project sufficiently popular and well-known in the applicable community?
- Is the project sufficiently mature?
- Is the product or version being evaluated a "release" version, e.g. not an alpha, beta, or comparable versions?
- Given the complexity of the project, does the project have a sufficient number of maintainers and contributors?
- Does the project keep its dependencies updated?
- Does the project have sufficient test coverage and do the tests include security relevant rules?
- Is the project well-documented and does the document include guidance on how to use the component securely?
- Does the project have an established and documented process for reporting vulnerabilities and are these vulnerabilities addressed in a timely manner?
- Is the intended usage of the project consistent with the project's license?

question: Django hands you a ready-made `django.contrib.auth` app for login/logout/password stuff, but FastAPI doesn't really have an equivalent. If I use FastAPI's `OAuth2PasswordBearer` helper, does it actually check that the token is legit, the way Django's auth app handles things for me?
answer: No. OAuth2PasswordBearer only checks the authorization scheme and pulls the bearer token out of the Authorization header — it does not validate the token or verify its signature. You still have to write your own authentication dependency that verifies the token and rejects invalid credentials before it returns a user. Django's django.contrib.auth, by contrast, already ships views/forms for login, logout, and password changes out of the box.
source_section: Dependency Injection and Access Control > OAuth2PasswordBearer Does Not Validate Tokens
source_passage: The helper class `OAuth2PasswordBearer` checks the authorization scheme and extracts the bearer token from the `Authorization` header. It does **not validate the token or verify its signature**. An authentication dependency must verify the token and reject invalid credentials before returning a user.

extra_sources.source_passage: Use `django.contrib.auth` app for views and forms for user authentication operations such as login, logout, password change, etc.

question: If I turn on allow_credentials=True for CORS in my FastAPI app, can I leave allow_origins as a wildcard to save time?
answer: No — once allow_credentials=True is set, you must explicitly list the trusted origins in allow_origins; you cannot combine credentialed requests with allow_origins=["*"].
source_section: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Configuration > Restrictive CORS Settings
source_passage: **Explicit Origins:** When using `allow_credentials=True`, explicitly list trusted origins in `allow_origins`. Do not combine credentialed requests with `allow_origins=["*"]`.

question: I want a Laravel rate limit that's keyed to the logged-in user's ID (falling back to their IP) at 5 requests a minute, instead of just using one of the default throttle numbers. How do I set that up?
answer: Define a custom limiter, typically in RouteServiceProvider, with RateLimiter::for('custom-limit', function ($request) { return Limit::perMinute(5)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip()); }); then attach it to the route with the throttle middleware, e.g. Route::middleware('throttle:custom-limit')->get('/dashboard', fn () => 'Dashboard').
source_section: Rate Limiting > 3. Custom Rate Limiter

question: In an Express app, if someone sends the query string `?foo[toString]=bar`, what does `request.query.foo` end up being — and why would that trip someone up?
answer: It becomes {} — an object where calling toString() on it will fail, because the query-string parser sets a 'toString' property on the object (shadowing the real method), rather than giving you a normal string or array like most other query shapes.
source_section: Recommendations > Application Security > Perform input validation
source_passage:
| URL | Content of request.query.foo in code |
| --- | --- |
| `?foo=bar` | `'bar'` (string) |
| `?foo=bar&foo=baz` | `['bar', 'baz']` (array of string) |
| `?foo[]=bar` | `['bar']` (array of string) |
| `?foo[]=bar&foo[]=baz` | `['bar', 'baz']` (array of string) |
| `?foo[bar]=baz` | `{ bar : 'baz' }` (object with a key) |
| `?foo[]baz=bar` | `['bar']` (array of string - postfix is lost) |
| `?foo[][baz]=bar` | `[ { baz: 'bar' } ]` (array of object) |
| `?foo[bar][baz]=bar` | `{ foo: { bar: { baz: 'bar' } } }` (object tree) |
| `?foo[10]=bar&foo[9]=baz` | `[ 'baz', 'bar' ]` (array of string - notice order) |
| `?foo[toString]=bar` | `{}` (object where calling `toString()` will fail) |

question: Besides the generic 'don't run untrusted code' warning, what's the specific mechanism that makes child_process.exec risky in a Node app?
answer: child_process.exec acts as a bash interpreter and sends its arguments to /bin/sh, so if attacker-controlled input gets injected into the command string you pass it, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the server — the same kind of remote-code-execution path that eval() opens when fed untrusted input.
source_section: Recommendations > Platform Security > Do not use dangerous functions
source_passage: There are some JavaScript functions that are dangerous and should only be used where necessary or unavoidable. The first example is the `eval()` function. This function takes a string argument and executes it as any other JavaScript source code. Combined with user input, this behavior inherently leads to remote code execution vulnerability. Similarly, calls to `child_process.exec` are also very dangerous. This function acts as a bash interpreter and sends its arguments to /bin/sh. By injecting input to this function, attackers can execute arbitrary commands on the server.

question: If my GraphQL API is only ever called by our own internal services, is it still fine to leave introspection and GraphiQL turned on in production?
answer: No -- disable introspection queries and GraphiQL (and similar schema-exploration tools) system-wide in any production or publicly accessible environment, regardless of whether the intended consumers are internal only.
source_section: Best Practices and Recommendations > Access Control
source_passage:
- [Disable introspection queries](https://lab.wallarm.com/why-and-how-to-disable-introspection-query-for-graphql-apis/) system-wide in any production or publicly accessible environments.
- Disable [GraphiQL](https://github.com/graphql/graphiql) and other similar schema exploration tools in production or publicly accessible environments.

question: In the batched GraphQL query example used to illustrate enumeration risk, how many different `droid` objects does the one request fetch, and how are they told apart since they're all hitting the same field?
answer: Three: `droid(id: "2000")`, `droid(id: "2001")`, and `droid(id: "2002")`. The second and third uses are labeled with the aliases `second:` and `third:` in the query.
source_section: Best Practices and Recommendations > Batching Attacks

question: What controls does the GraphQL cheat sheet list for resource-intensive queries and denial of service?
answer: Add depth limiting and amount limiting on incoming queries, add pagination, set reasonable timeouts at the application and/or infrastructure layer, consider query cost analysis with a maximum allowed cost per query, enforce rate limiting per IP or user, and implement server-side batching and caching (e.g. Facebook's DataLoader).
source_section: Best Practices and Recommendations > DoS Prevention
source_passage:
- Add depth limiting to incoming queries
- Add amount limiting to incoming queries
- Add [pagination](https://graphql.org/learn/pagination/) to limit the amount of data that can be returned in a single response
- Add reasonable timeouts at the application layer, infrastructure layer, or both
- Consider performing query cost analysis and enforcing a maximum allowed cost per query
- Enforce rate limiting on incoming requests per IP or user (or both) to prevent basic DoS attacks
- Implement the [batching and caching technique](https://graphql.org/learn/best-practices/#server-side-batching-caching) on the server-side (Facebook's [DataLoader](https://github.com/facebook/dataloader) can be used for this)
review_notes: Scoped the question to resource-intensive queries generally, since some listed controls (such as batching and caching) address overall work rather than nesting alone.

question: My RAG app currently logs the full retrieved chunks and the raw user query on every request so we can debug bad answers later - per the security guidance, is that fine to leave as-is?
answer: No. RAG Security's monitoring guidance says not to log raw queries, retrieved content, model inputs/outputs, or tool arguments by default, since they may contain secrets or sensitive personal data - trace requests instead with correlation IDs, retrieved document IDs, authorization decisions, model versions, etc., and only capture redacted content in a restricted evidence store if an incident genuinely requires it. This lines up with the Logging cheat sheet's general rule that things like access tokens, authentication passwords, and sensitive PII must never be written directly into logs - they should be removed, masked, hashed, or encrypted first.
source_section: Section 12: Monitoring and Incident Response > Do
source_passage:
- Trace each request using correlation IDs, retrieved document IDs, authorization decisions, model versions, and tool invocation outcomes. Do not log raw queries, retrieved content, model inputs, outputs, or tool arguments by default; these may contain secrets or sensitive personal data. Apply the [Logging Cheat Sheet's data-exclusion guidance](Logging_Cheat_Sheet.md#data-to-exclude).
- If incident investigation requires content capture, collect only the necessary redacted fields in a restricted evidence store. Apply [log access controls](Logging_Cheat_Sheet.md#protection) and [retention limits](Logging_Cheat_Sheet.md#disposal-of-logs), and ensure investigators are authorized to access the underlying documents.

extra_sources.source_section: Design, implementation, and testing > Data to exclude
extra_sources.source_passage:
The following should usually not be recorded directly in the logs, but instead should be removed, masked, sanitized, hashed, or encrypted:

- Application source code
- Session identification values (consider replacing with a hashed value if needed to track session specific events)
- Access tokens
- Sensitive personal data and some forms of personally identifiable information (PII) e.g. health, government identifiers, vulnerable people
- Authentication passwords

question: Roughly how much retrieved context - number of chunks and token budget - is a sane security-conscious default to stuff into the LLM's prompt per RAG query?
answer: A reasonable default in the RAG sheet is 3–5 retrieved chunks totaling about 2,000–4,000 tokens. The guidance says to limit both the number and total size of retrieved chunks to prevent context-window flooding.

question: Is it fine for my REST API to just send back the actual exception message or stack trace in the response body when something unexpected fails server-side, as long as the status code is a 500?
answer: No. Use the 5xx status code to indicate that the server couldn't fulfill the request, but don't include any response content that would reveal implementation details. Log the real error server-side instead and return a generic message to the client.
source_section: Objective
source_passage:
The article shows how to configure a global error handler as part of your application's runtime configuration. In some cases, it may be more efficient to define this error handler as part of your code. The outcome being that when an unexpected error occurs then a generic response is returned by the application but the error details are logged server side for investigation, and not returned to the user.

The following schema shows the target approach:

![Overview](../assets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet_Overview.png)

As most recent application topologies are *API based*, we assume in this article that the backend exposes only a REST API and does not contain any user interface content. The application should try and exhaustively cover all possible failure modes and use 5xx errors only to indicate responses to requests that it cannot fulfill, but not provide any content as part of the response that would reveal implementation details. For that, [RFC 7807 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7807) defines a document format.
review_notes: Expanded the Objective passage to include server-side logging and generic responses, which the original answer cited but the short excerpt omitted.

question: We're planning to fine-tune a shared LLM across several partner companies using federated learning so no one has to hand over their raw training data - what security controls does OWASP recommend for that setup?
answer: I don't know.
